article.Citation/Title: P. Glue, Cape, G., Tunnicliff, D., Lockhart, M., Lam, F., Hung, N., Hung, C. T., Harland, S., Devane, J., Crockett, R. S., Howes, J., Darpo, B., Zhou, M., Weis, H., & Friedhoff, L. (2016). Ascending single-dose, double-blind, placebo-controlled safety study of noribogaine in opioid-dependent patients. Clinical Pharmacology in Drug Development, 5(6), 460-468.
article.InterventionDescription: Single oral ascending doses of noribogaine (60, 120, or 180 mg) or matching placebo, given to opioid-dependent inpatients switched from methadone to morphine, confined at a clinical trials unit.

ae_events.Description: Noneuphoric visual impairment (light/colors perceived as brighter), onset ~1 hour postdose, resolved by 2.5-3 hours; commonest in 120- and 180-mg groups; no hallucinations reported.
Headache, reported across placebo and all active dose groups; most instances mild-moderate, one instance investigator-rated 'severe' in intensity; all AEs resolved before study completion.
Nausea, reported across placebo and active dose groups; most instances mild-moderate, one instance investigator-rated 'severe' in intensity; resolved before study completion.
Dose- and concentration-dependent QTcI prolongation, up to mean 42 ms at 180 mg; one 180-mg subject exceeded QTcI 500 ms at 4 timepoints, prompting DSMB dose-escalation caution.
Vomiting, one of three AEs investigator-rated 'severe' in intensity (with nausea and headache); no affected-participant count given; resolved before study completion.

article.EligibleYN: Y. Criterion (a): prospectively planned, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled ascending single-dose trial with defined enrollment (27 patients established on methadone OST), an assigned regimen (60/120/180 mg noribogaine or placebo), and prospective outcome assessment (Methods) -- clearly passes. Criterion (b), per instruction to judge on whether any opioid-use or withdrawal outcome is reported: this is not a pure PK/safety endpoint study -- Methods explicitly states 'Opioid withdrawal was evaluated' via time to resumption of OST and the validated SOWS/OOWS/COWS withdrawal scales (Results, 'Pharmacodynamics'), so a withdrawal outcome is reported and (b) passes. Both criteria met, so EligibleYN='Y' despite the study's title framing it as a 'Safety Study' and its primary designated endpoint (QTc) being a cardiac-safety measure, not an SUD outcome -- the withdrawal/OST-resumption data are secondary but sufficient for (b) per the boundary rule that a trial's only SUD outcome may be secondary.
article.Outcome: The article explicitly designates a 'primary end point': Results/Electrocardiographic Effects states 'QTcI was chosen as the primary end point because the average sum of squared slopes was somewhat lower for this correction than for QTcF.' Per the precedence rule (author-designated primary outcome beats the abstract-led SUD outcome or the largest of co-equal outcomes), Outcome is drawn from the QTc exposure-response analysis rather than the opioid-withdrawal secondary outcome. The single quantitative model parameter reported for this primary end point is the concentration-QTcI slope: 'The mean slope of the noribogaine/plasma concentration relationship was 0.17 milliseconds per ng/mL' (Discussion; also given in the Abstract). This is a discrepancy worth flagging: the study's only SUD-relevant secondary outcome (opioid withdrawal ratings/time to OST resumption) showed 'a nonstatistically significant trend toward decreased total score...most notably at the 120-mg dose' with the authors noting the design 'may have confounded' this analysis -- consistent with the codebook's depression-vs-drinking-days example, the primary-outcome rule routes Outcome to the non-SUD QTc finding even though this article is included in an SUD evidence review on the strength of its secondary outcome. Alternative candidate numbers considered and rejected as the 'Outcome' value: the by-dose-group mean DeltaDeltaQTcI effects (16/28/42 ms at 60/120/180 mg, Abstract/Results) and the model-projected effects at geometric mean Cmax (30 ms and 42 ms with 90%CI, Discussion) are all downstream restatements of the same concentration-response relationship rather than the single model parameter itself.
article.SD: 90%CI, 0.14 to 0.20 ms/ng/mL, printed in the same sentence as the 0.17 ms/ng/mL slope used for Outcome (Discussion, 'The mean slope of the noribogaine/plasma concentration relationship was 0.17 milliseconds per ng/mL (90%CI, 0.14 to 0.20 milliseconds)'). No SD/SE/F/t is reported for this specific regression slope; the CI is the only paired dispersion statistic given.
article.PVal: '.' -- no exact p-value or thresholded p-value is printed anywhere for the QTc concentration-response slope or the by-dose-group QTc effect. The article only characterizes the finding qualitatively as 'a clear, statistically significant dose- and concentration-dependent effect on the QTc interval' (Results) without ever printing a number or threshold alongside that claim, so per the rules this is coded not-reported rather than inferred as '<0.05'.
article.SampleSize_NFinal: 27, the full analyzed cohort (Results: 'Thirty-four subjects were screened, and 27...were enrolled in and completed the study'; 6 active + 3 placebo per dose level x 3 levels = 27). The exposure-response model for DeltaDeltaQTcI vs concentration uses time-matched concentration as a covariate with placebo-corrected DeltaQTcI as the outcome ('Subjects dosed with placebo were analyzed as a pooled group'), so both actively-dosed and placebo subjects contribute to the fitted model, but the article never states a single explicit analysis-population N for this specific model. The number of subjects contributing nonzero noribogaine concentrations is 18 (6 per active dose level); 27 is used here as the best-supported whole-study denominator, and this ambiguity is flagged rather than resolved by assumption.

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: All 14 elements are explicitly described in this industry-sponsored Phase 1 report. Objective is stated in the paragraph preceding Methods; design ('ascending single-dose, placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group study'), setting ('Zentech Clinical Trials Unit in Dunedin, New Zealand'), eligibility (methadone dose/duration, age, medical-clearance criteria), intervention (dose levels, timing, dosing procedure), comparator (matching placebo capsules), and outcomes (PK, PD, safety measures) are all in Methods. Sample_size_power is coded Y because, although no a priori power calculation is reported, the Discussion explicitly discusses the small-sample limitation ('likely to have been underpowered to identify uncommon or subtle safety findings'), which the codebook treats as sufficient description. Randomization ('computer-generated random code') and blinding ('double-blind') are explicit. Statistical methods, results, harms (dedicated Safety section and AE table), and funding/COI (separate Funding and Declaration of Conflicting Interests sections) are all fully reported.

article.Pos Result Y/N: 0. Judged against the study's own designated primary end point (QTc), the result is an adverse safety signal, not a positive treatment effect: noribogaine produced a dose- and concentration-dependent QTc prolongation reaching 'clinically concerning levels in the higher-dose groups' (Discussion) and prompted a DSMB-mandated reduction of the top planned dose from 240 mg to 180 mg. The study's only SUD-relevant outcome (opioid withdrawal/time to OST resumption) was likewise non-significant ('nonstatistically significant trend...however, the study design may have confounded evaluations'). Neither the primary nor the secondary outcome supports a positive-result code; 0 (null/negative) rather than 3, since directionality is not genuinely ambiguous -- QTc worsened and withdrawal was unchanged.
article.Ibogaine: 1. Per explicit task instruction, noribogaine is ibogaine's active metabolite (Introduction: 'ibogaine as being rapidly converted oxidatively to an active metabolite, noribogaine') and is the sole study drug administered in this trial. No other named psychedelic compound (psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, mescaline, MDMA, ketamine, cannabis) appears anywhere in the article, so only the Ibogaine flag is set and OtherPsychedelic/MultiplePsychedelic remain 0.
article.BaseStatus: '.'. Patients were 'established on methadone OST at 25-80 mg/day for at least 30 days' -- i.e., in stable maintenance treatment -- but no standardized severity classification (ASI composite, DSM severity specifier, or comparable measure) for opioid dependence is reported anywhere in the article, so severity cannot be coded without fabricating a threshold.
article.Age_Median: '30-50'. Results: 'Mean age was 41.2 years,' which falls within the 30-50 bracket.
article.PercentFem: 22.2. Results: '27 (21 male, 6 female) were enrolled.' 6/27 x 100 = 22.2%.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: 25.9. Results: 'Twenty subjects were white, 5 were Maori, and 2 were other.' Non-white = 5 + 2 = 7 of 27 = 25.9%. Arithmetic shown per the sum-non-white-groups rule.
article.SocioeconomicStatusYN: 0. No income, employment, insurance status, or other SES indicator is reported anywhere in the article.
article.Country_USvsNonUS: 'NonUS'. All sites and author affiliations are in New Zealand (Zentech Clinical Trials Unit, Dunedin; University of Otago; Southern District Health Board; University of Auckland) -- see Country field note; actual country is New Zealand.
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: 0. Participants were a screened Phase 1 volunteer population: eligibility explicitly excluded anyone with 'acute or serious chronic medical or surgical disorders,' and the protocol required confinement to the study site from 24 hours predose to 72 hours postdose plus outpatient follow-up -- a highly monitored, medically pre-screened inpatient sample atypical of routine community OST care.
article.InterventionTherapy: 0. No counseling, psychotherapy, or preparation/integration component is described; the intervention is a single pharmacological dose administered under inpatient PK/safety monitoring only.
article.CulturalFraming: 0. The Introduction's account of ibogaine's Bwiti religious/ritual origins ('Ritual eating of root bark is sacramental in the Bwiti religion...where it has psychedelic effects') is background on the substance, not an explicit framing of this trial's participants, methods, or findings around racial/ethnic identity or historical trauma. The demographic report that 5/27 participants were Maori (Results) is population reporting captured under RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent, not cultural framing of the study itself.
article.IndigenousFramework: 0, per the codebook's explicit instruction that describing a plant medicine's traditional origin in passing is not integration. The Bwiti/West African traditional-use background (Introduction) is mentioned only as context for ibogaine's discovery and is not referenced, incorporated, or drawn on anywhere in this trial's design, consent process, or interpretation.
article.ConfoundYN: 1. Discussion substantively discusses a specific confound: because active and placebo subjects within a cohort were housed together and observed continuously, 'restarting of OST would have been obvious to other participants, and this may have confounded any evaluation of dose-response for time to restarting OST' -- supported by the near-identical placebo-vs-active resumption times within cohorts (Pearson r=0.993, Results).
article.Followup in months: 1.25. Methods: 'there were subsequent outpatient and telephone assessments until 35 days postdose.' Since this is a single-dose study, end-of-treatment and dosing day are the same, so no baseline-vs-end-of-treatment discrepancy applies. 35 days = 5 weeks; converting at 4 weeks/month (matching the codebook's 2 weeks = 0.5 month convention) gives 5 x 0.25 = 1.25 months.
article.BehaviorChangeMeasured: 1. Time to resumption of OST and the SOWS/OOWS/COWS withdrawal-behavior ratings are behavioral/craving-adjacent outcome measures (Methods, 'Pharmacodynamic assessments...included...Opioid withdrawal was evaluated in several ways').
article.MentalHealthChangeMeasured: 0. COWS/OOWS/SOWS are physiological/subjective opioid-withdrawal symptom scales, not depression, anxiety, PTSD, or well-being instruments; no such mental-health scale is reported anywhere in the article.
article.RelapseMeasured: 1. 'Time to resumption of OST' is explicitly measured from the last morphine dose until participants resumed opioid agonist treatment (Methods) -- functionally a return-to-opioid-use/relapse-timing outcome, tracked as one of the study's core pharmacodynamic end points.
article.MortalityMeasured: 1. Safety section states explicitly 'There were no deaths or serious AEs,' confirming mortality was actively monitored and reported as zero rather than left unassessed, consistent with the rule that a reported death count (including zero, via AE surveillance) counts as measured.
article.SafetyReported: 'Y'. Dedicated Methods subsection ('Safety evaluations included...') and Results 'Safety' section with an AE table (Table 3) and explicit AE-severity narrative.
article.AnyAEReported: 'Y'. 'A total of 78 adverse events (AEs) were reported by 22 participants' (Results, Safety).
article.NumDistinctAEs: 'Not numbered'. The article names only 4 specific AE terms (visual impairment, headache, nausea, and vomiting, the last named only as one of the three AEs rated severe) out of 78 total reported AE occurrences across 22 participants; Table 3 is explicitly headed 'Most Commonly Reported Adverse Events,' implying additional, unnamed AE types make up the remainder of the 78 events. No full AE-type list or count of distinct types is given anywhere, so the total distinct-type count cannot be determined from the text.
article.ArmScope: 'pooled'. Table 3 reports AE-by-individual counts separately for Placebo (n=9), 60 mg, 120 mg, and 180 mg, and the headline '78 AEs...22 participants' figure sums across all four arms including placebo -- reported AE values are not restricted to noribogaine-exposed participants alone.
article.WorstSeverity: 'Severe', driven by the QTcI-prolongation event (ae_events AE04): see that event's rationale for why it is graded Severe under the rubric (FDA 'medically important event requiring intervention to prevent' a more serious cardiac outcome) despite the article's blanket statement that 'there were no deaths or serious AEs.' Absent that reinterpretation, the highest article-labeled AE severity would be the investigator 'severe'-intensity ratings for one instance each of headache/nausea/vomiting, which are graded Moderate here per rubric (see ae_events rationale) because they do not independently meet an FDA seriousness criterion.
article.Retention (%): 100. Study was randomized; Results states 27 patients 'were enrolled in and completed the study,' with no reported loss between randomization (27) and completion (27). Randomized N = completed N = 27, so retention = 27/27 x 100 = 100%.
article.Power: 1. No a priori power calculation is reported, but Discussion explicitly states the small sample size is 'likely to have been underpowered to identify uncommon or subtle safety findings,' which the codebook treats as sufficient to count power as discussed.
article.PrimaryCare: 0. The trial was conducted at a dedicated clinical trials unit with inpatient confinement; participants requesting OST resumption were 'released to the care of the local OST clinical service' post-discharge, which is specialty addiction treatment rather than a primary-care interface.

ae_events.P. Glue 2016_AE01: Onset coded 'post-session-acute' rather than 'in-session': there is no discrete psychotherapy-style 'session' in this PK/safety trial, but the effect's reported timing (onset within 1 hour postdose, resolved by 2.5-3 hours -- Safety section) fits the hours-scale definition of post-session-acute more literally than 'in-session'. Severity 'Mild' and SeveritySource 'author' both taken directly from the text: 'Visual impairment was the term used to describe noneuphoric changes in light perception of mild intensity.' NAffected=13 summed from Table 3 across all four arms (2 placebo + 2 at 60 mg + 5 at 120 mg + 4 at 180 mg).
ae_events.P. Glue 2016_AE02: Severity judgment call: the Safety section states one headache instance was among 'Three AEs...rated as severe (nausea, vomiting, and headache); all others were rated as mild-moderate in intensity,' but the same paragraph also states 'There were no deaths or serious AEs.' Because the article's own mild/moderate/severe wording is an informal intensity scale rather than a CTCAE grade or an SAE flag, and the authors explicitly disclaim any serious AE, this instance is graded Moderate (not Severe) under the rubric's Grade-3-equivalent default ('Moderate...unless it meets an FDA seriousness criterion'), rather than accepting the literal word 'severe' at face value -- SeveritySource is therefore 'rubric', not 'author'. No specific onset timing is given for headache individually (only visual impairment has an explicit timing description), so Onset is coded 'unknown'. NAffected=13 summed from Table 3 (5 placebo + 4 at 60 mg + 2 at 120 mg + 2 at 180 mg).
ae_events.P. Glue 2016_AE03: Same severity-mapping judgment as AE02 applies (one nausea instance was investigator-labeled 'severe' but the article also states no serious AEs occurred; graded Moderate, SeveritySource='rubric'). NAffected=5 summed from Table 3 (1 placebo + 0 at 60 mg + 2 at 120 mg + 2 at 180 mg). Onset coded 'unknown' -- no per-AE timing given for nausea.
ae_events.P. Glue 2016_AE04: This event is not tabulated in Table 3 ('Most Commonly Reported Adverse Events') alongside headache/visual impairment/nausea/vomiting, and the article's blanket Safety-section statement is 'There were no deaths or serious AEs' -- which would argue for a non-severe grade. However, Results (Electrocardiographic Effects) reports that QT prolongation observed after the first two dose cohorts led the independent DSMB to recommend reducing the planned top dose from 240 mg to 180 mg, and that in the 180-mg group '1 subject had a QTcI value exceeding 480 milliseconds at 1 time, and 1 subject had QTcI > 500 milliseconds at 4 points,' with one subject each in the 120- and 180-mg groups also crossing the pre-specified ΔQTcI > 60 ms safety threshold (Methods). This is graded Severe here (SeveritySource='rubric', overriding the article's blanket 'no serious AEs' summary) because a DSMB-mandated dose de-escalation specifically to avert a more serious cardiac outcome meets the FDA seriousness catch-all ('a medically important event requiring intervention to prevent one of the above') and QTc > 500 ms is a recognized torsades-risk threshold; MeetsFDASerious and InterventionRequired are both coded 'Y' on this basis. This is flagged as the most consequential and least obvious severity call in this record and should go to human review: it directly contradicts the article's own summary sentence, and the cardinal principle here is that understating this signal would be the worse error given it is explicitly the article's 'most notable safety finding' (Discussion) and drove a protocol-level dose change. NAffected is coded '.' because the specific subject counts given (>480 ms once; >500 ms x4 timepoints; ΔQTcI>60 ms once each in 120-/180-mg groups) may refer to overlapping or distinct individuals and cannot be safely summed into one unique-participant count from the text.
ae_events.P. Glue 2016_AE05: Vomiting is named only once, as one of the three AEs 'rated as severe (nausea, vomiting, and headache)' (Safety section); no dose-group breakdown or affected-participant count is given for vomiting specifically (it does not appear as a row in Table 3, which lists only headache/visual impairment/nausea). NAffected is coded '.' accordingly. Same severity-mapping logic as AE02/AE03 applies: graded Moderate rather than Severe given the article's explicit 'no...serious AEs' statement and the informal (non-CTCAE) nature of the authors' intensity scale; SeveritySource='rubric'. Onset coded 'unknown' -- no timing is given for vomiting.

config_proposal.metric: Exposure-response linear mixed-effects regression slope (change from baseline, placebo-corrected QTcI vs. plasma noribogaine concentration)
config_proposal.note: The article's designated primary end point is a concentration-QTc regression slope from a linear mixed-effects exposure-response model, not one of the seven supported conversion methods (d, g, eta_p, F, chi2, OR, RR); no defensible conversion to Hedges' g exists. Direction is set to -1 because the slope's natural sign (QTc lengthening with increasing noribogaine concentration) is an adverse cardiac-safety signal, opposite to a favored SUD-treatment-benefit direction, even though the statistic itself is not being converted.
config_proposal.tier2_basis: The article's only SUD-relevant outcome -- opioid withdrawal ratings (SOWS/OOWS/COWS) and time to resumption of OST -- showed a nonstatistically significant trend toward reduced withdrawal at 120 mg, and near-identical placebo-vs-active time-to-OST-resumption within cohorts (Pearson r=0.993), which the authors attribute to a design confound (shared housing/observation making OST resumption obvious to co-housed participants) rather than to a genuine null effect. No SUD outcome reached significance in either direction.
